pages.title: Management of power: balance of power assumptions
pages.summary: The three ways to manage power are balance of power, deterrence and collective security. Balance of power is a realist, militaristic concept called an axiom of international politics, which David Hume called common sense, and it rests on anarchy, security dilemma and self-help, pursued through internal or external balancing.

pages.title: Balance of power: conditions, techniques, liberal critics
pages.summary: Internal balancing is more reliable than external, and the ideal conditions are a regional setting with 5-6 major powers ready to fight for sovereignty. Traditional techniques include arms race, alliances, war and buffer zones, while liberals such as Woodrow Wilson and Nehru call balance of power a nervous state of peace.

pages.title: Why balance of power's relevance is questioned
pages.summary: The ideal conditions ceased after the Second World War: the bipolar world made states satellites, bandwagoning became better than balancing, and nuclear weapons produced a Balance of Terror based on MAD. In the unipolar twenty-first century states prefer soft balancing, and terrorist actors fall outside the traditional concept.

pages.title: Asymmetrical balancing and balance of power conclusion
pages.summary: Realists coined asymmetrical balancing for nations cooperating against non-state actors. The conclusion says balance of power survives in regional settings, where states acquire conventional weapons to avoid blackmail by regional hegemons, citing the USA's Asia Pivot and India's Act East Policy.

pages.title: Deterrence: meaning and types
pages.summary: Deterrence is a realist, psychological policy based on game theory and rational actors, meant to frighten an adversary so that he does not attack, and it leads to arms race. Its types include conventional and nuclear, denial and punishment, direct and extended, and massive retaliation (Eisenhower, India's policy) versus flexible response.

pages.title: Flexible response and relevance of deterrence today
pages.summary: Flexible response was Kennedy's concept, favouring short-range technical weapons. Nuclear deterrence remains central after the Cold War, with more nuclear states and a new arms race, the 1995 US Strategic Command document, the 2002 US National Security Strategy and the Bush Doctrine of preventive war against Iraq.

pages.title: Post-Cold War doctrines still rely on deterrence
pages.summary: The US Nuclear Posture Review 2010, NATO's 2012 Deterrence and Defence Posture Review, Russia's 2016 National Security Strategy and a revived French nuclear doctrine all rely on deterrence. The conclusion is that no major power has reduced reliance on nuclear deterrence.

pages.title: Collective security versus balance of power
pages.summary: Collective security is a liberal idea first proposed by Woodrow Wilson, meaning all for one and one for all. It shares balance of power's assumptions but is an institutionalised, more assured form that needs an international organisation, whereas balance of power is ad hoc and based on common sense.

pages.title: Limits of collective security; League of Nations record
pages.summary: Collective security is called utopian because states follow national interest rather than peace. The League failed because every country had a veto, aggression was undefined, USA and USSR stayed out, and it took no action over Manchuria in 1931 or Ethiopia in 1936; under the UN only P-5 consent is needed.

pages.title: Collective security in Korea; Uniting for Peace; peacekeeping
pages.summary: East-West conflict paralysed collective security, and Korea in June 1950 was the only Cold War example, stopped by a Soviet veto. The Uniting for Peace (Acheson Plan) resolution lets two-thirds of the General Assembly authorise action, and peacekeeping, a Dag Hammarskjold idea outside the Charter, is said to show collective security's failure.

pages.title: Collective security after Cold War; peacekeeping debate
pages.summary: The Gulf War was the best example, with over 30 countries under US leadership, but the UNSC has since been polarised between P2 and P3, and Responsibility to Protect arose for intra-state conflicts. Peacekeeping is becoming dangerous, with developed countries funding it while developing countries supply the troops.

pages.title: Developing countries' view; India and UN peacekeeping
pages.summary: Developing countries object that the Security Council does not consult the true contributing countries. The page lists points on India's peacekeeping record, says participation strengthens India's claim to a permanent UNSC seat, and notes a lack of enthusiasm for peacekeeping under the present government.

pages.title: Collective security versus collective defence (NATO)
pages.summary: India opposes collective defence pacts like NATO because they undermine collective security and show no faith in the UN system. The USA sees no contradiction, citing Article 51 on self-defence, and notes collective defence is only for members while collective security is universal.

flashcards.front: What realist assumptions underlie the balance of power, according to the notes?
flashcards.back: International politics is in a state of anarchy, nations suffer from the security dilemma, and self-help is the way of survival. The notes compare it to Newton's law of gravity and cite David Hume calling it common sense.

flashcards.front: What is the Balance of Terror, and why did traditional balancing techniques fail after the Second World War?
flashcards.back: The bipolar world ended the ideal conditions of regional politics, 5-6 powers and conventional wars, and made satellites of states, so bandwagoning beat balancing. Nuclear weapons then produced a Balance of Terror or Nuclear Balance between the superpowers based on MAD.

flashcards.front: What is asymmetrical balancing, and which examples show balance of power still operates?
flashcards.back: Realists coined it for nations cooperating against non-state actors. The notes cite the USA's Asia Pivot or re-balance and India's Act East Policy as examples of balance of power logic.

flashcards.front: What are the main types of deterrence, and which doctrine did Eisenhower propose?
flashcards.back: Types include conventional and nuclear, denial and punishment, direct and extended, and massive retaliation versus flexible response. Deterrence by punishment needs second strike capacity, and massive retaliation, Eisenhower's concept, targets civilians to inflict unacceptable damage.

flashcards.front: Which post-Cold War US documents and actions show continued reliance on nuclear deterrence?
flashcards.back: The 1995 US Strategic Command document Essentials of Post Cold War Deterrence, and the 2002 National Security Strategy, which promised sophisticated delivery systems and kept old hardware operational. The Bush Doctrine also used preventive war against Iraq to stop rogue nations acquiring weapons of mass destruction.

flashcards.front: How does collective security differ from the balance of power?
flashcards.back: Collective security is an institutionalised form of balance of power, whereas balance of power is ad hoc and based on common sense. It can exist only when an international organisation exists, and liberals call it a more assured state of peace than a nervous one.

flashcards.front: Why did collective security fail under the League of Nations?
flashcards.back: Every country had a veto, the Charter did not define aggression, and USA and USSR were outside the League. Britain and France saw USSR as a bigger enemy than the Fascist powers, and the League took no action over Japan in Manchuria in 1931 or Italy in Ethiopia in 1936.

flashcards.front: What is the Uniting for Peace resolution and why was it needed?
flashcards.back: Also called the Acheson Plan, it lets two-thirds of the General Assembly authorise collective security action when the Security Council is deadlocked, as happened over Korea in 1950. USSR never accepted its legality, so it became harder to operationalise.

flashcards.front: How do India and the USA differ on collective defence pacts like NATO?
flashcards.back: India says such pacts undermine collective security and show no faith in the UN system. The USA says there is no contradiction because Article 51 recognises the right of self-defence and collective defence is a practical way to operationalise collective security.

answers.question: Is the balance of power still relevant in the twenty-first century? Discuss.
answers.intro: Balance of power, called an axiom of international politics and compared to Newton's law of gravity, rests on anarchy, security dilemma and self-help. Its relevance is questioned because its ideal conditions have ceased to exist since the Second World War.
body: Its ideal conditions are a regional setting, five to six major powers ready to fight for their sovereignty, and conventional wars, using arms races, alliances, counter-alliances, war, partition and buffer zones; internal balancing is more reliable than external balancing.
Liberals such as Woodrow Wilson and Nehru reject it as offering only a nervous state of peace, and critics say it inoculates against measles but gives rise to plague.

After the Second World War the bipolar world turned states into satellites, so bandwagoning became better than balancing, while nuclear weapons produced a Balance of Terror based on Mutually Assured Destruction.
In the twenty-first century a unipolar world favours soft balancing over hard balancing, and terrorism has produced asymmetrical balancing, where nations cooperate against non-state actors.
Regionally it persists: the USA's Asia Pivot or re-balance and India's Act East Policy show balancing logic, and conventional wars have not become out of context altogether.
answers.conclusion: Balance of power no longer works in its ideal form, yet states still acquire conventional arms to resist regional hegemons, so it keeps relevance in regional settings. Its future lies in soft and asymmetrical balancing alongside nuclear deterrence.

answers.question: Examine the working of collective security under the United Nations. Why has it been difficult to operationalise?
answers.intro: Collective security, a liberal idea first proposed by Woodrow Wilson, means all for one and one for all and is an institutionalised form of balance of power. The notes trace it from the League of Nations to the United Nations.
body: The League of Nations failed through conceptual flaws: every state held a veto, aggression was undefined, USA and USSR were absent, and it took no action over Japan in Manchuria in 1931 or Italy in Ethiopia in 1936.

Under the UN only P-5 consent is needed, yet East-West conflict paralysed it; Korea in June 1950 was the only Cold War example, stopped by a Soviet veto. The Uniting for Peace resolution lets two-thirds of the General Assembly authorise action, but USSR never accepted its legality.

After the Cold War the Gulf War was the best example, with over 30 countries under US leadership, but US-Russia conflict returned and the UNSC is polarised between P2 and P3. Responsibility to Protect emerged because present conflicts are intra-state.

Peacekeeping, a brainchild of Dag Hammarskjold and not in the Charter, is itself said to show collective security's failure and is now more dangerous, with developed countries funding it and developing countries supplying troops.
answers.conclusion: Collective security has worked only rarely, constrained by great-power rivalry, vetoes and the shift to intra-state conflict. Peacekeeping, Responsibility to Protect and fairer consultation with troop contributors, including India, are the practical routes to more credible UN security action.
